interest: FBI surveillance of a Japanese naval language officer, 1940–41.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.3211, with related confidential filings under 894.7211) documents the diplomatic notifications, status inquiries, and internal security surveillance concerning Lieutenant Masakazu Tukasaki (also recorded as Masakusu Tukasaki and Masakato Tukasaka), an Imperial Japanese Navy ordnance officer stationed in the United States as a language student between October 1940 and September 1941. Beginning with official diplomatic notes from the Japanese Embassy announcing Tukasaki's arrival and correcting his naval title, the file traces an inquiry by FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover regarding whether Tukasaki enjoyed diplomatic immunity. Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr. confirmed that Tukasaki lacked immunity but urged the FBI to exercise discretion during surveillance to protect American naval language officers stationed reciprocally in Japan. The file concludes with an extensive FBI investigative report compiled in August 1941 after Washington Metropolitan Police discovered four bullet holes and suspected blood stains in Tukasaki's automobile parked behind the Alban Towers, detailing his interrogations, university studies at the University of Pennsylvania and Catholic University, nationwide travels, and eventual departure for Tokyo via Seattle in July 1941.

subfiles.about: Comprehensive FBI internal security report on the investigation of Japanese naval officer Masakato Tukasaka (Masakazu Tukasaki) after bullet holes were found in his car.
subfiles.from: W. J. Goodwin, Special Agent, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.summary: Special Agent W. J. Goodwin submits an eight-page internal security report covering the period July 9 to August 8, 1941, regarding Japanese Ordnance Lieutenant Masakato Tukasaka (Masakazu Tukasaki). The investigation began when D.C. Metropolitan Police Officer Maurice Barco impounded Tukasaki's 1940 Buick coupe after finding four bullet holes and suspicious dark stains; Assistant Coroner Dr. Rosenberg determined the stains were not blood. Tukasaki and his roommate Siuichi Shinohara were questioned by police, the FBI, Immigration Inspector W. P. Glendening, and ONI representative Lee Shipman, with Tukasaki claiming the damage occurred while the car was parked near the Alban Towers during his trip to the Shenandoah Valley with Captain Ichiro Yokoyama and other Japanese naval officers. The report inventories materials found in the car and his residence, details his academic enrollments at the University of Pennsylvania and Catholic University, charts his extensive automobile tours throughout the United States, and notes his scheduled departure for Tokyo via Seattle on July 18, 1941, concluding with the closure of the case due to a lack of evidence of activities inimical to U.S. security.
subfiles.title: FBI investigative report by Special Agent W. J. Goodwin on Masakato Tukasaka (Masakazu Tukasaki)
